title: Overshooting the Coordinate: Where Factor Corrections Land on Characteristic Axes

p.t: Maximum-Sharpe spanning asks how much a factor expands the mean-variance opportunity set, not where it leaves pricing errors along the economic coordinate from which it was constructed. This distinction matters for low-dimensional factor models: a factor can improve the attainable Sharpe ratio while leaving systematic alphas on a restricted return subspace. Spanning criteria compare factor spaces without locating those errors (Barillas andShanken, 2017, 2018;Fama and French, 2018). GRS and characteristic-sorted tests instead evaluate supplied test assets and can pool portfolios across anomaly families into a joint pricing restriction (Gibbons et al., 1989;Lewellen et al., 2010;Giglio et al., 2025). Their conclusions, however, depend on the chosen assets and bins, and they do not use the full economic order within a characteristic to show whether a correction stops short of, reaches, or overshoots zero. This paper develops a characteristic-axis integral diagnostic for that missing question. Fix a characteristic before observing test-period returns, sort stocks by it, and at each cutoff p form a cap-weighted prefix portfolio. Subtracting equal exposure to the aggregate of the same valid subuniverse produces a zero-investment bridge D x t (p) with model alpha α x m (p). Varying p traces a pricing-error curve over the entire order. Together with a zero-alpha aggregate gate, a zero bridge curve prices every prefix excess return and the tail, interval, and step-function returns generated by the axis; if the gate fails, the restriction applies conditionally to the internal zero-investment bridge subspace. Signed area records direction, while IAE, ISE, and the sup norm measure total, concentrated, and local distortion. Once the characteristic, order, and traversal measure are fixed, the full path is generated mechanically rather than selected through a small number of bins. 1I apply the diagnostic to value, operating profitability, investment, and momentum in 1967-2024 CRSP data. Models without the relevant counterpart factor generally leave positive pricing-error curves, while counterpart-factor content shifts them downward. Where those corrections land differs sharply. HML-based models push the value curve through zero into significantly negative errors, with rank alphas near -28 bp. Investment-factor models also cross zero, although their negative errors receive only marginal support under monthly HAC inference and selected 5% rejections under the moving-block bootstrap. RMW and UMD instead bring profitability and momentum close to zero. Adding UMD to FF3, for example, moves the momentum rank alpha from +92.6 to -7.1 bp, with no functional rejected at 5%. Momentum therefore provides a positive control: the diagnostic recovers known factor content and can produce a nearly flat curve when the correction aligns with the coordinate.

A comparison with conventional decile tests, extended to the market-capitalization benchmark of Shin (2026), shows that the axis results are not obtained by applying a uniformly more aggressive test. Across 30 model-axis cells, decile GRS and axis IAE agree in 20, including ten joint rejections and ten joint non-rejections; the remaining disagreements divide evenly between five GRS-only and five axis-only rejections. On value, FF5 and FF6 pass both the ten-decile GRS test and the extreme-decile spread but are strongly rejected by the axis diagnostic, which detects a broad negative distortion through the interior of the book-to-market order. On momentum, Carhart and FF6 are strongly rejected by GRS and the extreme spread but not by rank area or IAE, because their remaining decile errors are localized and nonmonotone rather than cumulative along the coordinate. The capitalization benchmark exhibits both directions of disagreement within one order: FF3, FF5, and FF6 are rejected only by the axis diagnostic, whereas q5 is rejected only by the conventional decile tests. GRS therefore retains broader scope over arbitrary finite asset sets and crossanomaly joint restrictions, while the axis diagnostic gives up that omnibus role to obtain deeper, order-aware resolution within one prespecified coordinate. The results also show why frontier expansion and axis destination are complementary rather than interchangeable. High covariance fit does not guarantee a flat coordinate: FF5 explains approximately 76% of the value-axis payoff and is nevertheless rejected on it. Nor does a large maximum-Sharpe gain determine where a correction lands. Across 155 candidate factors, q EG produces the largest increase in the attainable Sharpe ratio yet leaves large value-and investment-axis errors, whereas more coordinate-specific factors with smaller Sharpe gains bring those axes closer to zero. The appraisal ratio measures the potential scale of a factor's contribution, but the signed alignment of its residual with the axis and the model's starting curve determine whether the coordinate remains undercorrected, is flattened, or is pushed beyond zero.

Inference is model-specific because each nonlinear functional is calibrated to the residual covariance of that model's bridge regressions. A noisier residual curve produces a wider null distribution, so non-rejection can reflect weak resolution rather than favorable pricing. I therefore report each functional with its model-specific 5% threshold q 95 and the rank-area R 2 Y . On momentum, q5's IAE of 17.8 bp lies below the tighter thresholds attained by Carhart and FF6, indicating that its small point estimate is not solely an artifact of a loose null. On value, by contrast, q5's IAE of 22.2 bp exceeds the 19.0 bp threshold at which FF5 is rejected, making its non-rejection less informative. Finite-sample calibration confirms that these resolution differences are quantitatively important. The pricing-error curves belong to traded factor implementations, not to characteristics in the abstract. Within FF5, removing HML makes the value rank alpha more negative, from approximately -28 to -40.6 bp, so HML mitigates rather than generates the distortion. Rebuilding each counterpart factor as a univariate spread likewise moves the four axes differently. The alternative investment factor lowers IAE from 14.4 to 8.5 bp and moves the rank alpha from -12.5 to +6.7 bp; the conventional investment-decile GRS p-value simultaneously rises from 0.0186 to 0.291. Alternative profitability and momentum constructions instead move their previously flatter axes away from zero, while the alternative value factor leaves the value curve significantly negative. The same characteristic signal can therefore shift an axis differently depending on how it is packaged into a traded portfolio.

Factor replication, conventional-decile comparisons, moving-block bootstrap inference, and finite-sample calibration weaken explanations based on merge errors, accounting timing, critical-value approximation, or size distortion. The claims remain local. At the population level, the aggregate gate and zero bridge curve price only the subspace generated by the chosen characteristic order; empirically, non-rejection means only that no distortion is detected at the implemented grid and resolution. The procedure examines one characteristic at a time and provides neither a global model ranking nor an omnibus cross-axis restriction. Within those limits, it reveals what spanning and finite sorted portfolios do not jointly provide: where a factor correction lands along the full coordinate it was built to price. 2 Factor Spanning, Test Assets, and Characteristic-

Factor spanning and the missing diagnostic question. The proliferation of multifactor models has made model comparison central to empirical asset pricing. Fama-French, Carhart, and q-factor models explain overlapping return patterns using different factor sets and economic motivations (Fama and French, 1993;Carhart, 1997;Fama and French, 2015;Hou et al., 2015Hou et al., , 2019Hou et al., , 2020Hou et al., , 2021Hou et al., , 2024)). For traded-factor models, Barillas andShanken (2017, 2018) show that relative mean-variance comparison can be reduced largely to factor spanning and the associated maximum Sharpe ratio rather than repeated evaluation on arbitrary common test assets. Fama and French (2018) approach factor selection from the same perspective, while Kozak et al. (2018) emphasize that much SDF-relevant information is concentrated in a small number of return directions. This paper takes the spanning criterion as given and asks a complementary question. Maximum-Sharpe spanning measures whether a factor expands the attainable opportunity set, but not where it leaves pricing errors on a prespecified economic coordinate. The factor's appraisal ratio governs the potential scale of its contribution, while its signed residual alignment with the axis and the model's starting curve determine whether the correction stops short of zero, reaches it, or overshoots it. Characteristic-axis pricing therefore complements rather than overturns spanning: one evaluates frontier expansion, while the other localizes errors on a restricted economic subspace.

Test assets and characteristic-axis diagnostics. Standard specification tests evaluate pricing errors on a selected return cross-section, including the GRS test (Gibbons et al., 1989), Hansen-Jagannathan distance (Hansen and Jagannathan, 1997), and SDF-based tests of linear factor models (Cochrane, 2005). Their conclusions necessarily depend on the supplied test assets. Lewellen et al. (2010) show that characteristic-sorted portfolios with strong common factor structure can make models appear more successful than they are, while Giglio et al. (2025) formalize the joint problem of weak factors and highly correlated exposures and propose supervised selection of informative assets. Repeated search across assets and specifications adds data-snooping concerns (Lo and MacKinlay, 1990), and replication studies document sensitivity to factor definitions, portfolio construction, and sample choice (Hou et al., 2020;Jensen et al., 2023). Recent work responds by constructing richer or more informative test-asset cross-sections. Kirby (2020) uses managed portfolios to reveal nonlinear characteristic-expected-return relations, and Bryzgalova et al. (2025) use decision trees to select portfolios that capture interactions and span relevant return variation. The axis diagnostic instead fixes one char-acteristic, ordering direction, and traversal measure ex ante. Conditional on those choices, the researcher does not select bins or optimized splits: the order mechanically generates the full prefix path. Thus, while Barillas andShanken (2017, 2018) remove arbitrary common test assets from relative mean-variance comparison, the present design reduces arbitrariness within a coordinate-specific specification diagnostic.

At each cutoff, the bridge removes equal exposure to the characteristic-valid aggregate before alpha estimation. The null is therefore a zero pricing-error curve over the internal bridge subspace rather than high explanatory power for a few sorted portfolios. Together with a zero-alpha aggregate gate, it prices the prefix, tail, interval, and step-function returns generated by the order. The diagnostic does not rank models globally; it identifies where a given model prices or misprices a prespecified coordinate that spanning alone does not localize. Characteristics, factors, and traded implementations. Many empirical factors originate from firm characteristics. Size and book-to-market organize the Fama-French threefactor model (Fama andFrench, 1992, 1993); momentum is a distinct return-continuation pattern (Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993;Carhart, 1997); and investment and profitability are central to later models (Titman et al., 2004;Novy-Marx, 2013;Fama and French, 2015;Hou et al., 2015). Whether characteristics proxy for priced covariances or describe expected returns directly remains unresolved (Daniel and Titman, 1997). I do not attempt to settle that debate. I condition on a characteristic as an economic coordinate and ask how a factor model's pricing errors are distributed along its order, allowing high covariance fit and systematic mean errors to coexist. The four empirical axes are established return coordinates rather than newly proposed anomalies. Value follows the book-to-market and anomaly-decomposition literature (Fama andFrench, 1992, 2008); investment follows the asset-growth evidence of Titman et al. (2004) and the investment factor of Hou et al. (2015); profitability is related to gross profitability (Novy-Marx, 2013), RMW (Fama and French, 2015), and the ROE and expected-growth factors in the q-model family (Hou et al., 2015(Hou et al., , 2021)); and momentum follows Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) and Carhart (1997). The contribution is not to rediscover their averagereturn spreads, but to test where factor corrections leave the full orders those characteristics define.

The relevant correction belongs to the traded factor implementation, not to the characteristic in the abstract. The 2×3 size-balanced designs of Fama andFrench (1993, 2015) and the multidimensional sorts of Hou et al. (2015) package characteristic information while controlling size and diversifying individual-stock noise, but they were not designed to minimize a pricing-error curve on the underlying coordinate. Factors built from similar signals can therefore have different appraisal ratios, residual alignment, and axis destinations. Related work shows that characteristic-sorted portfolios combine priced and unpriced risk (Daniel et al., 2020); heuristic sorts, characteristic weights, and cross-sectional slopes need not span the individual-stock SDF (Kozak and Nagel, 2023); and anomaly results vary with breakpoints, screens, and variable definitions (Fama and French, 2008;Hou et al., 2020;Jensen et al., 2023;Soebhag et al., 2024). An axis rejection therefore concerns a particular traded construction rather than the characteristic or broader model family. Section 5.9 tests this distinction by repackaging the same signals and measuring how the curves move.

Mechanically generating the test-asset path does not make inference equally informative across models. Because each functional is calibrated to the residual covariance of that model's bridge regressions, a noisier residual curve produces a wider null distribution and a looser critical value. I therefore report model-specific 5% critical values and the rank-area R 2 Y , while treating the latter only as a resolution diagnostic; Section 6.4 evaluates the resulting finite-sample asymmetry directly. The functional view. Portfolio sorting can itself be understood as nonparametric estimation. Cattaneo et al. (2020) formalize characteristic-sorted portfolios as partitioning estimators and show that statistically appropriate portfolio counts may exceed the conventional five or ten, while Kirby (2020) studies nonlinear characteristic effects through regression-based managed portfolios. Those papers estimate expected-return functions associated with firm characteristics. I instead estimate a factor model's pricing-error function on the cumulative bridge portfolios generated by a fixed order. At cutoff p, the estimand is the bridge alpha α x m (p); signed area measures direction, IAE total absolute distortion, ISE quadratic concentration, and SU P the largest local error. The restriction is therefore zero alpha on the characteristic-axis subspace generated by the full path, not on a selected collection of bins.

The cap-axis diagnostic of Shin (2026) measures pricing errors inside the market portfolio as a function of capitalization rank. Its essential ingredients are more general: a characteristic fixed before returns are observed, a universe sortable by that characteristic, and an implementable aggregate portfolio on the same universe. The resulting characteristic-axis diagnostic turns the destination of a factor correction into a zero-curve restriction: it asks whether the pricing-error path remains on one side of zero, is flattened, or is pushed beyond it. This section defines that diagnostic and relates its curve shifts to maximum-Sharpe spanning.

Let x be a stock-level characteristic observed at formation date τ (t), and let I x τ (t) be the set of stocks for which it is valid. This set may be smaller than the investible market; accounting axes, for example, are defined on the valid CRSP-Compustat subuniverse. The membership rule and characteristic order must use only information available at formation. Sort stocks in descending order of x i,τ (t) and assign each stock a strictly positive initial portfolio weight. A useful family is which includes cap weighting (ρ = 1) and equal weighting (ρ = 0). Initial weights are normalized to one and carried forward as buy-and-hold positions. The characteristic order remains fixed during the holding period, while the start-of-day portfolio values induce the current traversal measure. Suppressing this time dependence in the rank notation, let u ∈ [0, 1] denote cumulative current portfolio mass along the fixed order. Thus p is a portfoliomass cutoff, not necessarily a cross-sectional characteristic quantile. Let r x t (u) denote the simple return at rank u. The corresponding characteristic-valid aggregate return and its excess return are Under cap weighting, R A,x t is the value-weighted aggregate of the valid-characteristic universe. It coincides with the investible market only when that valid universe coincides with the market; otherwise it remains an implementable subuniverse portfolio.

For factor model m with factor vector f m,t , estimate The function p → α x m (p) is the characteristic-axis bridge-alpha curve. Thus SA is the alpha of a long-short portfolio with linear rank weights 1 2 -u: it is long the high-characteristic side and short the low-characteristic side, with intensity increasing toward the endpoints. Changing the traversal measure changes these portfolio weights but not the logic of the construction.

For a fixed characteristic universe, order, and admissible measure, define Assumption 1 (Regularity). All test returns and factor returns have finite second moments, and Var(f m ) is nonsingular. Definition 1 (Admissible measure). A formation-date measure is admissible if its initial weights use only information available at τ (t), place strictly positive mass on every valid stock, have finite total mass, and evolve thereafter only through the returns on the predetermined holdings. The power-of-cap family in (1) is admissible for every ρ ≥ 0. Proposition 1 (Restricted characteristic-axis pricing). Under Assumption 1, model m prices every return in V x if and only if Proof. For any square-integrable excess or zero-investment return R, the OLS alpha functional is Under Assumption 1, this is a bounded linear functional. Necessity follows because the generators belong to V x . For sufficiency, (15) sets the functional to zero on every generator. Linearity extends the result to finite linear combinations, and continuity extends it to their closed span. The proposition is a population statement. Because C x t (p) -pR f t = D x t (p) + p R A,x t , the aggregate gate and zero bridge curve jointly price every prefix excess return; differences of prefixes generate interval portfolios, and (5) generates tails. The restriction is therefore complete within V x , but says nothing about industry, other-characteristic, or idiosyncratic directions outside that space. This is a coordinate-specific specification requirement, not a statement about the size or mean-variance quality of the factor span. Expanding the attainable mean-variance frontier does not by itself imply that the pricing-error curve is zero on V x .

Remark 1 (Measure choice and the canonical implementation). The proposition holds for any admissible measure, but the resulting axis depends on that measure. The characteristic determines the order; the measure determines traversal, aggregate weighting, and rank-area portfolio weights. Cap weighting is canonical because it produces the value-weighted aggregate of the valid universe and approaches the investible market interpretation as coverage approaches one. Equal weighting is another admissible axis, not an invariant version of the cap-weighted test. The empirical analysis fixes ρ = 1 throughout. Remark 2 (Interpreting aggregate-gate failure). If α m ( R A,x ) ̸ = 0, a zero bridge curve prices only span{D x (p) : p ∈ [0, 1]}, not the full space V x . For accounting axes, aggregate alpha may partly reflect selection into the valid CRSP-Compustat universe. Results for gatefailing models are therefore interpreted conditionally as statements about the internal zeroinvestment bridge subspace.

The population restriction ranges over all p ∈ [0, 1]. I approximate it using a finite stock universe and a prespecified grid P = {p 1 , . . . , p L }, so non-rejection means that no distortion is detected at the implemented grid resolution. The empirical analysis uses the cap measure. Let w x i,t be the start-of-day buy-and-hold wealth share of stock i on holding day t, with N x t i=1 w x i,t = 1. Stocks retain their formationdate characteristic order. Define and for p ∈ (0, 1] let k t (p) = min{i : c x i,t ≥ p} and s t (p) = c x kt(p),t , with k t (0) = s t (0) = 0. The whole-stock bridge and midpoint rank-area return are The bridge longs a whole-stock prefix and shorts the same realized aggregate exposure. Because the boundary stock is not split, s t (p) may exceed p, although closure at both endpoints remains exact. The grid-integrated bridge and midpoint rank-area return therefore need not coincide exactly. I test SA through the rank-area alpha and report the difference as wholestock boundary approximation error. Across all six models and four axes, the absolute gap never exceeds 0.63 bp per year, with a median of 0.39 bp, two orders of magnitude below the distortions studied here. At each grid point I estimate (6) and collect the intercepts in α x m , whose ℓth entry is α x m (p ℓ ). The empirical integration weights and grid maximum produce the finite-grid versions of IAE, ISE, and SU P .

p.s: From maximum-Sharpe gains to axis destination
p.t: Two properties guide the empirical analysis. First, the signed shift is invariant to factor rescaling: multiplying g by a nonzero constant changes IR g and the residual correlation in offsetting ways, leaving the alpha shift unchanged. Axis distortion therefore cannot be reduced by reporting the same factor in smaller units. Second, both IR g and residual alignment belong to the traded portfolio rather than the characteristic in the abstract, so portfolios formed from the same signal can produce different shifts and destinations. Section 5.9 tests this distinction by repackaging the same characteristic information. In the empirical tables, underlies the appraisal-ratio results of Gibbons et al. (1989) and Barillas and Shanken (2017). ∆SA follows the signed convention 4 Data and Methodology I use daily CRSP stock returns (CRSP, 2026), Compustat annual fundamentals (Compustat, 2026), the Fama-French Data Library (French, 2026), q-factor provider data (Global-q.org, 2026), and Global Factor Data (Global Factor Data, 2026). The construction proceeds through three nested universes: a month-end capitalization and liquidity screen defines the CRSP investible universe; a daily capitalization screen produces the common clean market and internal return cM KT ; and each formation date restricts that market to stocks with a valid value, profitability, investment, or momentum signal. For accounting axes formed in June of year Y , I require f year = Y -1 exactly; investment additionally requires f year = Y -2. Firms with older fundamentals are dropped rather than carried forward, and the same convention governs the factor replications in Section 6.2. All tests cover January 1967-December 2024 (N = 696), but formation inputs are staged earlier when needed: the 1967 accounting portfolios inherit June 1966 formations, and January 1967 momentum uses returns beginning in January 1966. No reported regression includes returns before 1967.

p.s: CRSP investible universe and production clean market
p.t: The base sample contains NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ common stocks from January 3, 1967 through December 31, 2024. At each month-end, capitalization and average dollar volume over the previous 63 trading days determine investibility, with asymmetric entry and exit thresholds to reduce boundary turnover. 4 The screen retains 77.6% of common stocks on average while preserving approximately 99.7% of market capitalization and dollar volume. At year-end 2024 it contains 2,426 of 3,804 stocks and preserves 99.78% of capitalization and 99.28% of dollar volume. Within this universe, let E t contain stocks with positive lagged capitalization and an observed adjusted return. Ordering them by lagged capitalization, the production clean market C t is the smallest whole-stock prefix reaching χ = 0.9975: The boundary stock is retained in full. This characteristic-neutral screen supplies the common formation mask and an internal market benchmark; it is distinct from the buy-andhold characteristic-valid aggregate used in each bridge. cM KT correlates 0.999778 with the Fama-French market and 0.999799 with the q5 market, with daily RMSEs of 2.21 and 2.10 bp. Its candidate-model regressions have R 2 > 0.999 and insignificant Newey-West 21-day alphas. The benchmark models are CAPM, FF3, Carhart, FF5, FF6, and q5. FF6 adds momentum to FF5, while q5 contains market, size, investment, return-on-equity, and expectedgrowth factors. Baseline tests use published monthly factors, aligning the testing horizon with factor construction and reducing short-horizon nonsynchronous-trading concerns.foot_4

To vary factor packaging while preserving the characteristic signal, I construct univariate counterparts from Fama-French one-dimensional value-weighted portfolios. For book-tomarket, operating profitability, and investment, the reconstructed factors are the published 30/70 spreads with investment signed conservative-minus-aggressive. Because prior-12-2 momentum is distributed as deciles, I define This compares the upper and lower 30% of the momentum order, although the decile returns are formed separately and then equally averaged. Each reconstruction retains the sorting variable, breakpoint convention, value weighting, and formation schedule, but removes the explicit small-big split and cross-size averaging of the canonical 2 × 3 factor. It therefore changes several portfolio-design features simultaneously and is interpreted as alternative packaging, not as a clean causal test of size neutralization. Replacement specifications include either the canonical factor or its reconstruction, never both.

At formation date τ , axis x restricts the production clean market to stocks with positive market equity and a valid characteristic: Formation-date capitalization is renormalized within I x τ , so stocks without valid signals enter neither the rank path nor its aggregate short leg. The resulting R A,x t is an axis-specific buyand-hold aggregate and generally differs from daily reconstructed cM KT t , especially for accounting axes with incomplete Compustat coverage. Before testing the bridge curve, I estimate The cM KT regressions validate the common market implementation; this aggregate gate asks whether the model prices the characteristic-valid universe itself. If it fails, bridge results are interpreted conditionally on the internal zero-investment subspace.

At formation, the engine applies characteristic validity to the clean market and sorts surviving stocks by the predetermined signal, breaking ties by descending market equity and ascending PERMNO. The universe and order remain fixed through the holding period: July-June for annual accounting axes and the next calendar month for momentum. Prefix membership at a fixed mass cutoff may still change as buy-and-hold wealth shares evolve. 6The baseline path uses 201 equally spaced cutoffs on [0, 1]. At each date, the first wholestock prefix reaching target p is selected and the same realized aggregate exposure s t (p) is shorted. Every run verifies endpoint closure, body-tail recombination, and agreement between the integrated bridge and midpoint rank-area alpha; the latter differ by at most 0.63 bp per year across all models and axes. Daily bridge and rank-area payoffs are accumulated within each month: Arithmetic accumulation is appropriate because these are zero-investment payoff increments. The positive-wealth aggregate is instead compounded: Monthly bridge regressions then use the corresponding published monthly factors.

For each model-axis pair, I report the rank-area alpha, IAE, √ ISE, and SU P , together with their p-values, model-specific 5% critical values, and R 2 Y . The candidate-factor scan adds each of 155 monthly factors separately to CAPM and records its maximum-Sharpe gain and resulting axis distortion; the reconstructed factors are excluded from this library. Finally, the replacement experiment substitutes each reconstructed counterpart factor while holding the tested axis and remaining model fixed. These exercises distinguish frontier expansion, coordinate-specific correction, and sensitivity to traded factor implementation.

This section applies the monthly characteristic-axis diagnostic to value, operating profitability, investment, and momentum, corresponding to HML, RMW/ROE, CMA/IA, and UMD. The cap axis is studied in Shin (2026). Table 5.1 reports the valid-characteristic aggregate gates. CAPM, FF5, FF6, and q5 pass all four; FF3 and Carhart fail selected accounting-axis gates, whereas every momentum gate passes. As in Remark 2, bridge results for gate-failing models are interpreted conditionally on the internal zero-investment subspace. Note: Monthly bridge-alpha curves within each valid-characteristic universe. The horizontal axis is cumulative cap-weight share along the characteristic order; alphas are annualized basis points. Vertical scales differ across panels; cross-axis magnitudes should be compared using the functionals in Table 5.2-Table 5.5.

The value axis sorts stocks each June from high to low by requiring positive book equity and December market equity, and holds the order from July through the following June. The valid universe covers 81.2% of investible capitalization on average and 87.9% at the final formation date. Carhart fails the aggregate gate, while FF3 lies at the 5% boundary. Panel A of Figure 5.1 and Table 5.2 show a sign reversal. CAPM leaves an insignificant positive rank-area alpha of +24.3 bp, whereas FF3, Carhart, FF5, and FF6 leave significantly negative rank alphas near -28 bp and reject every nonlinear functional. HML-based models therefore push the value curve through zero rather than flattening it. Their high R 2 Y values, 0.743-0.760, show that covariance fit and elimination of mean pricing errors are distinct requirements. q5 also lies below zero but is not rejected against its wider threshold. Its IAE of 22.2 bp exceeds the 19.0 bp threshold faced by FF5, so its non-rejection is weaker evidence of flatness than the tightly estimated FF5 and FF6 results. CAPM's non-rejection is weaker still given its 47.8 bp threshold. These comparisons do not attribute the negative curve to HML alone.foot_6

The operating-profitability axis sorts stocks each June from high to low by and holds the order from July through the following June. Revenue must be observed and book equity positive; missing COGS, XSGA, and XINT are set to zero. The valid universe covers 81.3% of investible capitalization on average and 87.9% at the final formation date. FF3 and Carhart fail the aggregate gate. CAPM, FF3, and Carhart leave positive OP-axis curves near the 5% boundary. This is the only axis on which the functional choice changes the 5% verdict: FF3 is rejected by rank area, IAE, and √ ISE but not by SU P , while Carhart is rejected only by IAE. Because FF3 and Carhart fail the aggregate gate, these are conditional bridge-subspace statements. Table 5.7 summarizes the monthly rank-area alpha and IAE for the six benchmark models. The destination differs by coordinate. HML-based models cross into significantly negative value errors; investment-factor models also cross zero, but with only marginal monthly HAC-GP evidence. FF5 and FF6 flatten operating profitability, while Carhart and FF6 flatten momentum. Factor content therefore predicts the direction of correction more reliably than whether the resulting curve is tightly centered at zero. No benchmark model dominates. FF5 and FF6 produce the flattest profitability curves but are rejected on value, and FF5 leaves a large momentum distortion without UMD. Carhart is comparatively close to zero on investment and momentum but is rejected on value and remains marginal on profitability. q5 is not rejected at 5% on any axis under HAC-GP, although its value and investment distortions remain economically nontrivial and the moving-block bootstrap rejects selected investment functionals. High covariance fit is likewise insufficient: HML-based models are rejected on value despite high R 2 Y , whereas q5 passes momentum with R 2 Y = 0.134. The strength of non-rejection depends on model-specific resolution. On momentum, q5's IAE of 17.8 bp is below FF6's tighter 23.4 bp critical value, so its small point estimate is not merely an artifact of a loose null. On profitability, q5's 19.5 bp distortion is approximately equal to FF5's 19.5 bp threshold. p.s: Maximum-Sharpe gains do not determine where corrections land
p.t: Maximum-Sharpe contribution and axis destination are connected but not equivalent. By ( 26) and ( 24), the absolute appraisal ratio determines frontier expansion and scales the potential correction, while residual alignment and the starting curve determine its sign, shape, and destination. For the fixed CAPM benchmark, ∆SR is strictly increasing in |IR g |. Across the 155 factors, its Spearman correlation with IAE is +0.045 on value, +0.034 on momentum, -0.362 on profitability, and -0.344 on investment; the corresponding Pearson correlations are +0.313, -0.215, -0.213, and -0.318. Frontier gains are therefore nearly rank-unrelated to distortion on value and momentum and only moderately aligned on profitability and investment. The difference between Pearson and Spearman correlations, especially on momentum, also rejects a stable linear or monotone mapping from one criterion to the other. The starting curve helps explain these average patterns. CAPM begins with a relatively small value-axis IAE of 24.1 bp, so a large correction can cross zero and increase absolute distortion. Investment and momentum begin at 49.7 and 72.1 bp, leaving more room for a correction to reduce error. Even within an axis, however, frontier contribution does not identify the factor that produces the flattest destination. q EG has the largest ∆SR in the library, 1.240, yet leaves IAE of 61.8 bp on value and 39.8 bp on investment. Factors with much smaller gains-BE/ME, OPE/BE, NOA GR1A, and ret 12-7-leave substantially flatter curves on their respective coordinates. Maximum-Sharpe gains measure the potential scale of a correction; residual alignment and the baseline curve determine where it lands.

These objects depend on the factor portfolio and base model, not on the characteristic alone. 6 Robustness Checks I first benchmark the characteristic-axis results against conventional decile GRS and highminus-low tests. The comparison is not a horse race between substitutes. GRS can pool portfolios across anomaly families and test their joint alphas under the full residual covariance structure, whereas the present diagnostic deliberately studies one predetermined characteristic at a time. It gives up cross-axis scope to obtain order-aware resolution within the return subspace generated by that coordinate. I then assess implementation and inference through factor replication, moving-block bootstrap inference, finite-sample calibration, and grid-covariance diagnostics.

p.s: Conventional decile tests and axis diagnostics
p.t: For each axis, I estimate ten value-weighted decile alphas, their conventional GRS joint test, and the alpha of the extreme high-minus-low spread using the same monthly sample and factor models as in the axis analysis. The comparison includes the market-capitalization axis studied in Shin ( 2026) and the four characteristic axes examined here. GRS tests an arbitrary joint alpha configuration over the supplied portfolios and is invariant to their ordering, whereas the axis diagnostic uses the order directly: its prefix path, rank-area payoff, and nonlinear functionals target pricing errors that persist or accumulate over cumulative capitalization mass. The comparison does not exhaust the role of GRS. Portfolios from multiple anomaly families can be pooled in one GRS system, allowing cross-anomaly residual covariance to affect an omnibus joint restriction. The current axis procedure instead examines one prespecified coordinate at a time and provides no corresponding cross-axis test. Its contribution is therefore deeper resolution within an order, not broader simultaneous coverage across orders. Across the 30 model-axis cells, GRS and axis IAE agree in 20: both reject in ten and neither rejects in ten. The remaining ten disagreements are exactly balanced. GRS alone rejects q5 on market capitalization, CAPM on operating profitability, FF5 on investment, and Carhart and FF6 on momentum; axis IAE alone rejects FF3, FF5, and FF6 on market capitalization and FF5 and FF6 on value. Neither procedure is therefore a uniformly more aggressive version of the other.

p.s: Conventional decile tests and axis diagnostics
p.t: The capitalization results display both forms of disagreement within the same economic order. FF3, FF5, and FF6 pass decile GRS but are rejected by rank area and IAE, indicating pricing errors that accumulate broadly across the size order without producing a strong joint decile rejection. q5 exhibits the reverse pattern: GRS and the extreme spread reject, while rank area and IAE do not, consistent with decile-level errors that do not form a persistent cumulative curve. The remaining disagreements have the same interpretation. FF5 and FF6 on value leave broad negative distortions through the interior of the book-to-market order even though conventional decile tests pass. Carhart and FF6 on momentum, and FF5 on investment, instead contain portfolio-level errors detected by GRS that do not accumulate into a large rank-area or IAE statistic. GRS is sensitive to arbitrary finite-dimensional configurations, including sparse, oscillating, and endpoint-specific errors; the axis statistics concentrate power on distortions structured by the predetermined order. The broad agreement is equally informative. Both approaches reject the models that leave the clearest value, profitability, investment, and momentum errors and accept models whose curves and conventional portfolios are jointly close to priced. GRS and the extremedecile spread also reach the same 5% decision in 28 of 30 cells, with exceptions only for Carhart on market capitalization and FF5 on investment. The factor-reconstruction results provide an additional common check. Replacing CMA with the univariate CMA ′ raises the FF5 investment-decile GRS p-value from 0.0186 to 0.291, lowers axis IAE from 14.4 to 8.5 bp, and moves the rank-area alpha from -12.5 to +6.7 bp. Alternative factor packaging can therefore improve both conventional and order-aware pricing, although the corresponding HML reconstruction leaves the value curve significantly negative.

p.s: Conventional decile tests and axis diagnostics
p.t: Overall, GRS retains broader scope over arbitrary finite test assets and cross-anomaly joint restrictions, while the axis diagnostic provides deeper within-coordinate resolution. Their conclusions coincide when misspecification is visible both in selected portfolios and across the cumulative order, and diverge when errors are either broadly distributed through that order or localized in a small number of conventional portfolios.

The accounting axes and factor replications use the same timing convention: at June Y formation, I select fiscal year Y -1, with investment growth additionally using total assets from Y -2. Using the same CRSP-Compustat merge, return accounting, annual formation schedule, and published breakpoints as in the main analysis, I reconstruct where Exact equality with the published series is not expected because of historical data revisions and detailed differences in book equity, delisting treatment, and reinvestment conventions. The replicated factors are diagnostics, not regression inputs: all reported bridge alphas use the published factors. Component portfolios provide the most direct check on stock assignment and portfolio formation, while factor-level correlations, betas, and intercepts assess the final long-short combinations. Factor correlations range from 0.943 to 0.970 monthly and from 0.908 to 0.961 daily, with betas of 0.913-1.018. Component correlations are uniformly higher, at 0.979-0.998 monthly and 0.979-0.997 daily. The -45.7 bp HML intercept shows that small component discrepancies need not cancel in the final spread, but cannot affect the value-axis results because those regressions use published HML. Overall, the component agreement substantially weak- ens explanations based on inconsistent merging, fiscal-year timing, breakpoint assignment, or portfolio formation. Momentum requires no corresponding accounting check because UMD uses neither Compustat data nor fiscal-year matching.

The zero-curve null is imposed through and each resample re-estimates the full regression grid. The procedures agree in 65 of 72 cells and in every value and momentum cell. All seven

Holding the empirical monthly factors, fitted loadings, and centered residual curves fixed, I simulate α x m (λ) = λ α x m , λ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, within the bootstrap environment of (42). The case λ = 0 measures size; positive values preserve each estimated curve's shape and location while scaling its magnitude. Because the alternatives remain model-specific, rejection frequencies are not common-effect-size comparisons across models or axes. For each λ, I generate 4,999 evaluation samples. HAC-GP critical values use an independent 50,000-draw Gaussian simulation, and bootstrap critical values use an independent set of 4,999 null resamples. Null rejection remains near 5% under both methods, and average rejection rises monotonically with λ. At λ = 1, HAC-GP rejection is 66.0% on value, 51.7% on investment, 56.5% on momentum, and 32.9% on profitability. The lower profitability average partly reflects the nearly flat FF5 and FF6 alternatives rather than a failure of the test. The FF6-q5 momentum comparison illustrates model-specific resolution. Their observed IAE values are similar, at 16.1 and 17.8 bp, but HAC-GP rejection at λ = 1 is 18% for FF6 and 4% for q5. FF6 has R 2 Y = 0.805 and a 23.4 bp critical value, versus 0.134 and 52.4 bp for q5. Because their planted curves differ in shape, the power gap is not attributable solely to covariance fit, but it confirms that similarly sized observed distortions can have sharply different evidentiary content. The calibration establishes local power against empirical-shape alternatives, not uniform power against every possible curve.

p.s: Rank deficiency of the grid covariance matrix
p.t: The 201 × 201 grid covariance matrix Ω x m is structurally singular. Endpoint bridges are identically zero, and adjacent interior bridges differ only through stocks near the moving cutoff, inducing substantial cross-grid dependence. The inference procedure accommodates this directly. IAE, ISE, and SU P require only a positive-semidefinite square root of Ω + /T , never its inverse; the only inversion is the small factor second-moment matrix Q m in (19). Moreover, Ω + -Ω F Ω F = 1.4 × 10 -10 , so the positive-semidefinite adjustment is numerically negligible. The bootstrap bypasses Ω entirely yet agrees with HAC-GP in 65 of 72 cells. Rank deficiency is therefore an expected feature of the bridge path, not evidence that numerical instability drives the results.

The robustness checks weaken explanations based on accounting implementation, Gaussian calibration, finite-sample size distortion, or covariance singularity. Factor and component replications closely track the published constructions; bootstrap and HAC-GP decisions agree in most cells; size remains near nominal and power rises with alternative strength; and the singular covariance matrix is handled without inversion. The remaining sensitivity is economically informative rather than mechanical: selected investment rejections depend on the inference procedure, and low-resolution specifications can have little power against distortions of the magnitude they actually exhibit.

Interpreting where corrections land. Counterpart-factor content generally shifts its characteristic-axis curve downward, but the destination differs across coordinates. RMW and UMD bring profitability and momentum close to zero, whereas HML-based models push value into significantly negative errors near -28 bp. Investment-factor models also cross zero, although their rank alphas of -12.5 to -19.7 bp receive only marginal support under monthly HAC-GP inference and selected 5% rejections under the moving-block bootstrap. The robust investment result is therefore a sign reversal and nontrivial negative curve, not uniform rejection across models and functionals. These outcomes separate the direction of correction from its destination. By (26), the appraisal ratio scales the potential movement, residual alignment governs its cutoff-specific transmission, and the starting curve determines whether the enlarged model remains undercorrected, becomes flat, or overshoots. A downward shift alone is therefore not evidence that the coordinate has been successfully priced. Nor can the destination be attributed mechanically to the factor sharing the coordinate's name. Removing HML from FF5 moves the value rank alpha from approximately -28 to -40.6 bp, so HML mitigates rather than generates the distortion. CMA, by contrast, supplies enough downward correction to carry the investment curve below zero. The axis diagnostic locates pricing-error structure; attribution requires addition, removal, or replacement experiments. Functional geometry and test resolution. The diagnostic treats pricing error as a function rather than a list of portfolio alphas. SA, IAE, ISE, and SU P measure direction, total absolute magnitude, quadratic concentration, and the largest local deviation. Similar signed areas may therefore conceal a smooth one-sided curve, an oscillating path with offsetting regions, or a localized peak. Reporting the full curve and all four summaries limits dependence on whichever functional happens to reject.

The few disagreements across functionals reflect this geometry. On operating profitability, integrated functionals detect broad moderate distortions that SU P does not, and a related pattern appears on investment. Inference also depends on precision: each nonlinear functional is calibrated to the model's own cross-grid residual covariance, so noisier curves face wider null distributions. Model-specific critical values are therefore necessary to distinguish a small curve from one measured too imprecisely to reject. Finite-sample calibration confirms that similarly sized distortions can have sharply different rejection probabilities, making non-rejection a joint statement about magnitude and resolution rather than an unconditional pass. Relation to spanning and existing tests. The characteristic-axis diagnostic complements rather than replaces existing criteria. Maximum-Sharpe spanning asks whether an added factor expands the attainable mean-variance frontier, GRS tests whether a model prices a supplied finite asset set, and the axis diagnostic asks whether zero alpha holds on the restricted return space generated by one predetermined order. These criteria evaluate different objects. The comparison with conventional deciles makes this distinction empirical. Across 30 model-axis cells, including the market-capitalization benchmark of Shin (2026), decile GRS and axis IAE agree in 20, with ten joint rejections and ten joint non-rejections; the remaining disagreements divide evenly between five GRS-only and five axis-only rejections. Value illustrates broad ordered errors that decile tests can miss, while momentum illustrates localized or nonmonotone decile errors that need not accumulate along the coordinate. The capitalization benchmark contains both patterns within one order: FF3, FF5, and FF6 are rejected only by the axis diagnostic, whereas q5 is rejected only by the conventional decile tests. The axis procedure is therefore neither a uniformly more aggressive nor a uniformly weaker version of GRS; the two tests concentrate power on different alternatives.

GRS also retains an omnibus role that the present diagnostic deliberately gives up. Portfolios from several anomaly families can be pooled in one GRS system, allowing their joint pricing errors and cross-anomaly residual dependence to enter a single restriction. The current procedure examines one coordinate at a time and provides no corresponding cross-axis joint test. Its contribution is deeper, order-aware resolution within that coordinate. Once the characteristic, ordering direction, traversal measure, and grid are fixed ex ante, the prefix path is generated mechanically, reducing bin-selection discretion without eliminating the prior economic choice of coordinate. Spanning remains distinct from both forms of specification testing. The factor scan shows nearly zero rank associations between ∆SR and IAE on value and momentum and only moderate negative associations on profitability and investment. q EG produces the largest frontier gain in the library while leaving substantial value and investment distortions, whereas several factors with smaller ∆SR leave much flatter curves. The appraisal ratio determines the potential scale of a correction, but residual alignment and the starting curve determine where it lands.

p.s: What a rejection identifies, and what it does not.
p.t: An axis rejection identifies failure of a particular traded model to price a particular restricted return space. Because the axis portfolios are cap-weighted while canonical factors may be size-balanced or formed through multidimensional sorts, the rejection may reflect a mismatch between factor construction and the coordinate-specific weighting scheme. Such a mismatch may explain the error, but it does not remove the error from the model's pricing problem. The rejection does not indict the characteristic in the abstract. Appraisal ratios and residual alignment belong to traded implementations relative to the remaining model. Reconstructing the counterpart factors materially moves all four curves: CMA ′ flattens investment, whereas RMW ′ and UMD ′ move previously flatter axes away from zero. The improvement from CMA ′ also appears in conventional investment-decile pricing, whose GRS p-value rises from 0.0186 to 0.291. Because reconstruction simultaneously changes cross-size aggregation, constituent weights, and residual returns, it does not isolate a single causal design feature. It establishes the narrower point that the same signal can produce a different destination when packaged as a different traded portfolio. Three scope restrictions remain. First, accounting-axis conclusions concern the valid CRSP-Compustat subuniverses, and gate-failing results apply only to the internal zeroinvestment bridge space. Second, the findings are model-by-axis specific and do not produce a global ranking or a cross-axis omnibus test. Third, population pricing concerns only the subspace generated by the chosen order, while empirical non-rejection means only that no distortion is detected on the implemented grid at the available resolution. Neither implies pricing of industries, unrelated characteristics, or idiosyncratic directions. This narrow completeness is the purpose of the diagnostic: to locate where a factor correction lands without claiming validity outside the space generated by the prespecified coordinate.

Maximum-Sharpe spanning measures how a factor expands the mean-variance opportunity set, not where it leaves pricing errors along the characteristic it is meant to price. This paper develops a characteristic-axis integral diagnostic for that complementary question. A characteristic fixed ex ante generates cap-weighted prefix portfolios across the full order; subtracting equal exposure to the aggregate of the same valid subuniverse produces a bridgealpha curve. Together, the aggregate gate and zero-curve restriction price the prefix, tail, interval, and step-function returns generated by the axis without requiring a small set of researcher-chosen bins. Counterpart-factor content generally shifts the curves downward, but the destination differs by coordinate. HML-based models push value into significantly negative errors near -28 bp. Investment-factor models also cross zero, although the evidence is marginal under monthly HAC-GP inference and reaches 5% only for selected block-bootstrap functionals. RMW and UMD instead bring profitability and momentum close to zero. Momentum provides the clearest positive control: adding UMD removes approximately 84-100 bp of signed distortion without significant opposite-signed overshooting. Neither covariance fit nor maximum-Sharpe contribution determines where a correction lands. Across 155 candidate factors, frontier gains are nearly rank-unrelated to distortion on value and momentum and only moderately associated with lower distortion on profitability and investment. The appraisal ratio scales the potential correction, but residual alignment and the starting curve determine whether the axis remains undercorrected, becomes flat, or overshoots. The destination also belongs to the traded implementation: removing HML makes the FF5 value curve more negative, while replacing canonical factors with univariate reconstructions materially moves all four axes and substantially flattens investment.

The interpretation remains local and resolution-dependent. A rejection identifies failure of a particular factor implementation on a prespecified characteristic-axis space, not global model failure or invalidity of the underlying premium. A population pass prices only the subspace generated by that order, while empirical non-rejection means only that no distortion is detected on the implemented grid at the available resolution. Within these limits, the diagnostic reveals what spanning alone cannot-where factor corrections actually land on the characteristics they are designed to price.
